planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in rich, well-drained, evenly moist soil in partial shade, giving afternoon shade in hot climates to prevent leaf scorch.

directions: Site in rich, humus-amended, well-drained soil that stays evenly moist, and give afternoon shade where summers are hot to keep the foliage from scorching. Venus is a three-way hybrid bred at NC State from Carolina, California, and Chinese sweetshrub species, and it opens dozens of magnolia-like, nearly pure white flowers with yellow and maroon central markings over a long spring-into-summer season, releasing a fruity, melon-and-strawberry fragrance unlike the typical wine-scent of straight Calycanthus floridus. Its rounded, dense habit needs only minimal shaping, and the long-lasting flowers work well cut for indoor arrangements. Excellent as a specimen or informal hedge near a path or entry where its unusual color and fragrance can be appreciated up close.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Aphrodite tolerates more heat and humidity than the straight species.

directions: Grow in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Aphrodite was bred at NC State specifically to hold up better in hot, humid summers than older sweetshrub selections. From April through August it produces an extended succession of unusually large, clear reddish-purple flowers with bright yellow-tipped inner petals, noticeably brighter and rounder than the muted maroon blooms of typical Carolina allspice, backed by a light, fruity fragrance. Deer generally leave it alone, and the glossy deciduous foliage provides a clean backdrop to the long bloom season. A strong choice for a shaded shrub border or foundation planting where extended color and fragrance are wanted from a single native-derived shrub.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; this cultivar blooms on both old and new wood, so pruning timing is far less critical than for the species.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, average-to-rich soil in partial shade to full sun. Selected and refined over nearly two decades by Spring Meadow Nursery, Simply Scentsational reblooms continuously from late spring through fall rather than flowering in a single spring flush like most sweetshrubs, thanks to its dual old-wood-and-new-wood bloom habit. The velvety, deep maroon, magnolia-shaped flowers carry a fragrance often described as pineapple and bubblegum, noticeably sweeter and fruitier than the wine-like scent of the species. Its rounded, densely branched habit stays tidy with little pruning, making it a strong long-season choice for a shaded mixed border where extended bloom and fragrance are priorities.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center

common_name: Beaver Creek Fothergilla (Dwarf Compact Fall-Color Witch Alder)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, organically rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; this dwarf selection does not come true from seed, so propagate only from cuttings.

directions: Site in moist, acidic, organically rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade for the strongest fall color, though it tolerates fairly shady conditions. A Roy Klehm selection of the native dwarf fothergilla, Beaver Creek grows into a tight, compact, mounded shrub with fragrant, apetalous white bottlebrush flower spikes opening before the leaves in April or May and lasting three to four weeks. Its thick, blue-green summer foliage turns a vivid red flushed with purple, orange, and yellow once cool weather arrives, one of the most consistent fall shows among the dwarf witch alders. Its small, tidy mature size makes it an easy fit at the front of a shaded foundation planting or shrub border where a full-size fothergilla would be too large.

common_name: Red Licorice Fothergilla (Brilliant Red Fall Foliage Witch Alder)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun for the most intense fall foliage color.

directions: Grow in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; more sun generally intensifies the fall color, but the shrub performs well and blooms reliably in a partly shaded woodland setting. A selection of the naturally occurring hybrid between dwarf and large fothergilla species, Red Licorice produces the typical honey-scented white bottlebrush flower spikes in mid-spring before leafing out, then delivers exceptionally saturated, glossy red fall foliage that outshines most fothergilla cultivars for depth of color. Its intermediate size and rounded, low-suckering habit fit well as a mid-height accent in a mixed shrub border or shaded native plant garden. Minimal pruning is needed; remove only dead or crossing wood after flowering.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; some direct sun helps flowering but variegation holds best out of hot afternoon sun.

directions: Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, keeping soil consistently damp since summersweet resents drying out. Discovered by South Carolina plantsman Mike Creel, this cultivar is grown chiefly for its foliage rather than its flowers: new leaves emerge speckled, flecked, and banded with cream to white variegation, settling into a lustrous dark green patterned with white as they mature. It still produces the species' fragrant white flower spikes in mid-to-late summer, but the real appeal is season-long ornamental foliage that brightens a shaded, damp corner of the garden. Occasionally a branch will revert to solid green; prune these out promptly to keep the variegation from being outcompeted.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade, giving supplemental water during dry spells.

directions: Grow in evenly moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade, favoring the shadier end of that range in hot climates. Einstein is named for its unusually long, twisting, curled white flower racemes, which stretch up to a foot and are said to resemble the namesake physicist's hair, releasing the same intense, sweet fragrance typical of summersweet through mid-to-late summer when few other shrubs are blooming. Its dense, compact form and golden-brown fall color make it a useful, well-mannered addition to a shaded foundation bed or rain garden. Bees and butterflies visit heavily during bloom, and the shrub tolerates periodically wet soil without difficulty.

common_name: Sugartina Crystalina Summersweet (Dwarf Compact White Clethra)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; this dwarf cultivar fits easily into smaller shaded beds where full-size summersweet would be too large.

directions: Site in consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; like all summersweets, it struggles in dry soil and rewards regular watering. A Proven Winners introduction bred for a genuinely dwarf, dense habit, Sugartina Crystalina keeps the fragrant, pure white, upright flower spikes of the species on a scaled-down plant that fits foundation plantings, small shaded courtyards, and mixed borders where full-size Clethra alnifolia would quickly outgrow the space. Flowers open in mid-to-late summer and draw steady pollinator traffic, and the compact form needs essentially no pruning to stay tidy. A reliable, low-maintenance choice for gardeners who want summersweet's fragrance without its typical size.

common_name: Long Spire Virginia Sweetspire (Extra-Long Fragrant Racemes)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; this selection tolerates full shade and clay better than most flowering shrubs.

directions: Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic, well-drained to periodically flooded soil in partial shade to full sun; Long Spire tolerates heavier clay and shadier conditions than most flowering shrubs, including full shade. This cultivar was selected specifically for its exceptionally long, drooping, fragrant white flower racemes, which stretch six to ten inches, well beyond the typical length of species Virginia sweetspire, giving arching sprays of bloom in early summer. Good heat tolerance and multicolored yellow, orange, red, and purple fall foliage round out its seasonal interest. Excellent for stream banks, rain gardens, and shaded low spots where soil stays consistently damp.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center

common_name: Shirley's Compact Virginia Sweetspire (Dwarf Midget-Leaf Sweetspire)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in bright shade to full sun, in containers or small beds where its miniature scale can be appreciated up close.

directions: Grow in moist, well-drained soil in bright shade to full sun; this dwarf selection adapts to a range of soil types and tolerates more shade than most flowering shrubs. Discovered by the late Shirley Speight at North Carolina's Biltmore House, Shirley's Compact is a true dwarf form of Virginia sweetspire, forming a tight, mounding clump of tiny, twisted, inch-long leaves rather than the larger foliage typical of the species. Its cream spring flowers are so small they're best appreciated with a hand lens, but the shrub still turns vivid red, orange, and purple in fall like its full-size relatives, and it attracts pollinating bees despite its diminutive blooms. Its small mature footprint makes it ideal for rock gardens, containers, and the front edge of a shaded border where a standard Itea virginica cultivar would be far too large.

common_name: Love Child Virginia Sweetspire (Compact Prolific-Blooming Sweetspire)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; this compact selection needs less room than larger Itea virginica cultivars.

directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; like other Virginia sweetspires it tolerates occasional wet soil without trouble. Bred from a controlled cross between Henry's Garnet and Sarah Eve, Love Child combines a compact, freely branching, rounded-to-upright habit with an especially prolific display of white, star-shaped, fragrant flower racemes in early summer. Its vigorous growth and strong red-maroon fall color give it multi-season interest on a plant sized for a foundation planting or smaller shrub border where larger sweetspire cultivars would crowd the space. Low-maintenance once established, it needs only an occasional post-bloom shaping cut to control size.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
